SOURCES.exact_title: Communicating Sequential Processes
SOURCES.exact_section_page_theorem_table_figure_: Abstract and§1; §7.7 Kahn; §7.8 Output guards; §7.9 Automatic termination; Conclusions and acknowledgments
SOURCES.claim_supported: Synchronous unbuffered rendezvous, guarded alternatives with arbitrary choice, and parallel composition of statically bounded processes. No shared mutable variables; no recursion or process-valued variables in the presented notation. Fairness is not generally promised by arbitrary choice.
SOURCES.contrary_evidence_if_any: The paper explicitly does not address a proof method or efficient implementation. It offers a partial conceptual notation with programming exercises, not a deployed crash/recovery/delivery guarantee. Static process bounds, absence of output guards and automatic termination impose expressiveness and compositional costs. Most examples remain unread.

SOURCES.exact_title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
SOURCES.exact_section_page_theorem_table_figure_: PartialOrdering559; ClockCondition560; OrderingEventsTotally560–562; AnomalousBehavior562; PhysicalClocks563–564; Appendix564–565; Acknowledgment565
SOURCES.claim_supported: Happened-before is a partial order of actual local/message events; scalar clocks preserve it in one direction. Total extensions depend on arbitrary clock/tie choices. External causal information may need explicit transport or sufficiently bounded physical clocks. The illustrated synchronization protocol requires all processes and halts on a failure.
SOURCES.contrary_evidence_if_any: The physical-clock theorem assumes bounded rates and recurring sufficiently timely messages over a strongly connected graph. No deployment timing envelope is established by the paper. Its informal statement that failure requires physical time is not a general impossibility theorem beyond the formal model.

SOURCES.date_version_edition: ACM TOCS 3(1), February 1985, pp.63–75. Received January1984; revised September1984; accepted7December1984.

Theorem1 permits a reachable state absent from the actual event order, arising in a valid permutation. Termination additionally needs marker delivery and initiation reachability.
SOURCES.contrary_evidence_if_any: No guarantee of historical wall-clock simultaneity, arbitrary non-FIFO/lossy transport, persistence or external-effect closure. Stable-property true implies truth at completion; false only establishes falsity at initiation.

mechanism_notes: StateObjects exchange messages under fail-restart assumptions. Developer Persist, Restore and ListVersions must implement durability correctly. Actions do not interleave with persistence or restore; actions may run concurrently with one another, so developer thread safety remains necessary.

Detached threads can continue after rollback. Communication must carry intercepted or manual dependency metadata; merge may reject stale messages. A barrier guards externally visible speculative effects.

The protocol adapts DPR asynchronous prefix recoverability: rollback includes peers and control flow. Recoverable boundaries close dependency graphs. Origin, failure and persistence counters track dependencies; commit ordering waits for predecessor persistence.

Recovery uses consensus or durable logging to order failure epochs. Its coordinator can be stateless while the cluster log must remain durable, for example Raft or reliable storage. It waits for participant recovery responses.
Section5.1 leaves each service responsible for excluding two current incarnations from simultaneously updating its persistent state. Rollback metadata does not discharge that obligation.

General replicated services with quorum or weaker recovery semantics are outside the presented design. Timers and frontend workflow features are omitted. Coarse dependencies can overapproximate and discard extra work.
evaluation_notes: Azure experiments use ten D8s VMs, 120-second runs and 10ms group commits. TravelReservation is based on DeathStarBench; Beldi/Boki baselines are simulated by disabling speculation, not measurements of the competing implementations.

The DARQ event-processing trace is driven at 50,000 events/s for120s. The 2PC evaluation exercises commit logic only, without actual data operations: one coordinator, four participants, eight clients, 30,000 transactions.
Recovery kills one Kubernetes node at30s; roughly10s restart time dominates. An instantaneous-rollback2PC experiment is a simulated best case; with64clients speculation leads to additional aborts.
Automatic interception gives about25% lower maximum throughput; manual metadata handling less than5% lower. Rare/expensive recovery is a source premise, not field prevalence evidence.

actual_observation.title: Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS
actual_observation.version: Current official documentation accessed2026-11-10; no immutable release version
actual_observation.claim: Dead-letter queues isolate repeated failures for analysis and redrive; they do not complete the underlying business work. Moving a message from a FIFO workflow can break the required semantic order. Standard-queue expiry uses original enqueue time while the displayed oldest-message age starts at the DLQ move; FIFO timestamp behavior differs.
actual_observation.limitations: Declared vendor semantics, not independent experimental evidence. Retry-count and retention configuration are workload choices. A small retry budget can quarantine transient failures, while indefinite retries can consume capacity and delay other work.
